sections.en:
¹ Concerning the Babylonian system of thirty stars, cf. Diodorus II, 30, 6; Boll, Sphaera, in the Index under λαμπροὶ ἀστέρες.
² Apollonius of Myndus, a disciple of the Chaldeans, is praised alone, as it seems, by Seneca, Quaest. Nat., VII, 4, 1; 17, 1.
³ Without doubt Artemidorus of Paros, whose doctrine concerning comets the same Seneca reports, Quaest. Nat., I, 4; VII, 13; cf. Pauly-Wissowa, Realenc., II, 1333. Bidez thinks that this astronomer of Paros is the Artemidorus whom the life of Aratus (p. 57, 31, Westermann = Maas, Comment. in Arat., p. 324, 13) testifies to have written the Phaenomena.
⁴ Concerning this chapter of Hermes Trismegistus, cf. Hephaestion of Thebes I, 23 (p. 91 Engelbrecht) and Catal., IV, p. 124, n. 2; 154.
⁵ Petosiris and Nechepso are known to all (cf. Catal., IV, p. 120 etc.), but we confess to have discovered nothing concerning the Egyptian astrologers Nechao and Cerasphorus.
⁶ A fragment of Timaeus, who is already praised by Vettius Valens (cf. n. 6), you will find in Catal., I, p. 97.

summary.headline: Thirty Bright Stars and Their Authorities
summary.text: Astrological discussion of exceptionally fortunate nativities, the influence of stars co-rising with the angles or Moon, and the activity of thirty bright stars, excluding Canopus. The account follows Ptolemy and reviews Babylonian, Chaldean, Egyptian, Hermetic, and other authorities on fixed stars and the rising of the Dog.
